title: Teacher Agent: A Knowledge Distillation-Free Framework for Rehearsal-based Video Incremental Learning
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a machine learning problem rather than an educational intervention: how to reduce catastrophic forgetting in rehearsal-based video class-incremental learning without relying on a conventional teacher network for knowledge distillation. The authors argue that standard distillation-based rehearsal methods are computationally expensive for video models and can be misled by inaccurate predictions from the previous-stage teacher, especially as tasks accumulate.

To solve this, the paper proposes a knowledge distillation-free framework called Teacher Agent. The approach replaces the previous teacher model with a lightweight teacher generator that produces soft labels, together with a self-correction loss that helps the model review old knowledge. The framework also includes a unified sampler that selects a fixed number of key frames from stored videos, improving memory efficiency while preserving representative content.

The method is evaluated on four video action recognition benchmarks: Kinetics-incremental, Something-Something V1, UCF101, and HMDB51. Results show improved accuracy and reduced forgetting compared with prior rehearsal-based incremental learning methods such as iCaRL, BiC, and vCLIMB TC, while using substantially fewer FLOPs and lower-resolution video inputs. The authors conclude that the proposed teacher-agent strategy can effectively replace distillation in rehearsal-based video incremental learning and may also transfer to image class-incremental learning.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed computer vision/machine learning methods paper on incremental video recognition, not an education intervention study. It does not evaluate a K-12 instructional technology or compare against human coaching, peer review, self-review, or usual classroom practice.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational impact measured in K-12 settings, and no student learning, teacher practice, or institutional outcome evidence is reported. The paper’s improvements are limited to video classification benchmarks and computational efficiency.
